title: STORY TIME: My entire training history
summary: NH retells his training history from age 14 (under 5 ft, ~100 lb, couldn't do a push-up) through three years of calisthenics, three years of bedroom dumbbells, powerlifting-influenced barbell training and a fat bulk to 240 lb, then a two-year slow cut to 210. His three lessons: optimal training is not required to start, slow patient progress lasts longest, and realistic natural progress looks slow.
claims: He started training at 14, under five feet and around 100 lb, after losing an arm-wrestling match to a skinny girl
His first training came from manga: push-ups and sit-ups; at first he couldn't do a single push-up or a leg raise
He began with knee push-ups and quarter-range crunches; 5-10 minute workouts left him cramping and needing 2-3 days to recover
For a very weak beginner, five minutes of knee push-ups can be the optimal workout; optimal is relative to what you can do
Most of your workouts will not be optimal; demanding perfection leads to paralysis by analysis and inactivity
From 14 to 17 he trained only calisthenics and went from 100 to 140 lb while growing a full foot
He believes lifting during puberty guided his growth so he didn't end up gangly
Obsession can trump optimisation: training a body part relentlessly even with poor methods can outdo someone doing it properly
As a teen he did an hour of abs every day; he still has a six-pack he no longer trains
Muscle built in the past mostly stays as long as you remain active
Don't wait for perfect conditions to start; start with whatever you can, like knee push-ups
Novices need freedom in their first years; his novice program is deliberately open-handed
His three years of self-directed calisthenics forged his discipline; a mentor would have made him complacent
At 17 he bought a 50 lb dumbbell set and started curling 5 lb dumbbells (after 2-3 lb pink and blue ones)
He trained two hours a day every day with no rest days for years because training gave him peace
He responds better to volume and long sessions than to intensity, though he needs both
Slow progress let his linear progression last about six years in total
Progressing from 0 to 200 slowly accumulates far more volume, experience and stamina than doing it fast and stalling
Bodybuilding is a game of patience
From 17 to 20 his dumbbell training took him from 140 to 170 lb
He trained in giant sets without rest, resting only 2-3 minutes at the end of each giant set with a timer while reading Hajime no Ippo
All his biceps size came from cheat curls, the only curl he did for about six years, kept low intensity so he never got hurt
YouTube teens gaining 50 lb of muscle in a year are either on drugs or getting fat
After moving countries, his first six months in a real gym went nowhere because he kept trying everything instead of focusing
Following powerlifters on YouTube brought big early progress on compounds
Years of calisthenics and dumbbells meant his first barbell sessions were a two-plate deadlift for reps, 150 lb bench and 185 lb squat with good form
From 21 to 23 he went from 170 to 240 lb; he was already fat by 210-220 but body dysmorphia hid it
Gaining weight fast makes you stronger but it is fat; he regrets those years the most
Lift with a clear goal; without one, progress itself becomes the goal and you lose the plot
He wishes he had gained only 15-20 lb from 20 to 23 to sit at a solid 190
Steady slow progress beats fast progress followed by stalls or regression
After a bad experience with a suicide cut, he cut slowly from about 235 to 210 over two years before starting the channel
Admit to yourself if you lift for physique; justifying it as functional causes problems
Since 25 he has stayed at the same bodyweight while measurements and strength rise slowly; it's his proudest progress
His 'final program' no longer changes; it has enough mechanisms to adapt continuously and he focuses on weak points
